title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 2: Not Easy to be a Cabinet Member
keywords: Not Easy to be a Cabinet Member
the things that money cannot buy
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's June 20, 2010 Inquirer column warning that it 'would not be easy to serve in the Cabinet of President Noynoy Aquino,' who, having promised to hold the Arroyos accountable, would demand of his own officials 'a very high standard of accountability and transparency'

The qualities a P-Noy Cabinet member needs -- trustworthiness, integrity and probity (TIP), the courage and humility of Ninoy and Cory, the absolute trust of the President as his 'alter egos,' and a willingness to surrender privacy to the world's freest media

The demands of confirmation and public life -- Commission on Appointments scrutiny, divestment, asset disclosure, simple living, and a working mastery of the Constitution, the Anti-Graft Law, the Ethical Standards Law and the Administrative Code

The model public servant -- Jovito Salonga, marking his 90th birthday, who dissolved his famed law office on joining Cory's Cabinet, and whose 'supreme teaching' prized 'the things that money cannot buy' (integrity, moral courage, honor, faith) over those it can
sub_topics: The premise: with 'many... jockeying for the choicest positions,' aspirants should realize that, because P-Noy 'promised to hold Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and her officials accountable,' he will want 'his own subalterns to pass a very high standard of accountability and transparency'

Teamwork, brainwork, hard work: under 'leadership by example,' Cabinet members 'should exemplify trustworthiness, integrity, and probity (TIP)' and the 'courage, humility, and heroism' of Ninoy and Cory -- as 'alter egos' who 'must instinctively know his mind,' like Mar Roxas, who shares 'the same mindset, the same vision,' subordinating personal ambition to teamwork

Forfeited privacy: officials 'should be ready to forego their privacy,' since the 'tri-media, the freest in the world,' will scrutinize 'the minutest details of their lives' -- they will be 'headlined, columnized, broadcast, texted, tweeted, YouTubed, and Facebooked' and be 'on call' around the clock

Confirmation's gauntlet: subject to Commission on Appointments confirmation, secretaries 'must be prepared to be interrogated about their public and private lives' -- past activities, taxes and ventures dug into 'to horse trade political and personal favors,' with 'long forgotten enemies' raising 'their slightest indiscretions'

The legal duties: they 'must leave their professions and divest from their businesses,' disclose assets and liabilities and list relatives 'by blood or by affinity' yearly, and -- since 'the Constitution requires them to live simply' -- be ready to explain how they acquired their houses and afford to send children abroad

Substance plus credibility: it is 'not enough to serve well, it is equally important to communicate well and to be credible,' for 'even the purest of officials must undergo public scrutiny' -- 'the price of public service' -- so they should keep an 'iPad or... memo book' with the Constitution, the Anti-Graft Law, the Ethical Standards Law and the Administrative Code

The Salonga exemplar: 'new public servants can take some lessons from the life of Dr. Jovito R. Salonga,' marking his 90th birthday -- who, on joining Cory's Cabinet, 'dissolved his famous law office,' giving up his 'only source of income' though 'not required by law,' 'to set a new standard in ethical conduct'

Salonga's standing and teaching: a 1944 bar topnotcher, Harvard and Yale graduate, professor and young law dean, author, congressman who 'trumped two dynasties in Rizal,' the only Filipino to 'top the Senate race three times,' and 'the best president the country never had' (losing to Ramos in 1992) -- CJP's 'lifetime guru' since 1956, whose 'supreme teaching' was that beyond 'the things that money can buy' we must aspire for what it 'cannot buy': 'integrity, moral courage, character, honor, humility, dignity, and an abiding faith in the love and mercy of God'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's June 20, 2010 Inquirer column, warns that it 'would not be easy to serve in the Cabinet of President Noynoy Aquino.' Because P-Noy 'promised to hold Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and her officials accountable,' he will demand of his own subalterns 'a very high standard of accountability and transparency.' Under 'leadership by example,' Cabinet members 'should exemplify trustworthiness, integrity, and probity (TIP)' and the 'courage, humility, and heroism' of Ninoy and Cory, serving as 'alter egos' who 'must instinctively know his mind' -- like Mar Roxas, who shares 'the same mindset, the same vision' -- and subordinating personal ambition to teamwork. They must 'forego their privacy' before the 'tri-media, the freest in the world' (to be 'headlined... tweeted, YouTubed, and Facebooked'), survive Commission on Appointments scrutiny of their 'public and private lives,' 'leave their professions and divest from their businesses,' disclose assets and relatives, and -- since 'the Constitution requires them to live simply' -- explain how they acquired their houses; it is 'not enough to serve well,' for 'even the purest of officials must undergo public scrutiny,' 'the price of public service.' CJP holds up Jovito Salonga -- on his 90th birthday -- who 'dissolved his famous law office' (his 'only source of income') on joining Cory's Cabinet, though 'not required by law,' 'to set a new standard in ethical conduct': a 1944 bar topnotcher, Harvard and Yale graduate, three-time Senate-race topnotcher and 'the best president the country never had' (losing to Ramos in 1992), and CJP's 'lifetime guru' since 1956. His 'supreme teaching': beyond 'the things that money can buy,' we must aspire for what it 'cannot buy' -- 'integrity, moral courage, character, honor, humility, dignity, and an abiding faith in the love and mercy of God.'
